newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran starts registering president poll candidates.
newsitem.headline: Iran starts registering president poll candidates.

text.p: Iran on Thursday began signing up candidates for next month's election to replace President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani in a campaign expected to focus on internal issues rather than foreign policy.
Tehran radio said the five-day registration period opened at the interior ministry for entrants in the May 23 poll.

The list of candidates would be handed over on Tuesday to the Guardian Council, a 12-man election screening body of lawyers and Shi'ite Moslem clerics, which would announce the approved candidates within 10 days, the radio said.
About a dozen candidates have said they would register to run in the election, Iran's seventh presidential poll since the country's 1979 Islamic revolution.
The Guardian Council has in past polls disqualified all but a handful of those who signed up after checking their allegience to Iran's Islamic system of government and religious leadership.
Iran's laws say only Shi'ite men can become candidates, but a female former member of parliament has said she would sign up to force a legal interpretation allowing women to run.

The election appeared to be shaping up as a two-horse race with Parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, backed by conservatives who hold a majority in the assembly and many bazaar merchants, facing Mohammad Khatami, a former minister of culture and Islamic guidance.
Khatami, like Nateq-Nouri a Shi'ite cleric, is backed by pro-Rafsanjani centrists and radical Islamist intellectuals who have moderated many of their views in the past few years.
Rafsanjani is barred by the constitution from running after two consecutive four-year terms. His mandate ends on August 3.
Analysts said Iran's foreign policy and its confrontation with the United States and Israel were not expected to become election issues.

"I do not think anyone in the Iranian leadership could at this time of confrontation with Washington propose any shift in foreign policies which are in the final analysis set by (Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali) Khamenei," one analyst said.
Khamenei has supreme power over all state institutions.
"Rafsanjani, because of his stature as an old guard of the revolution, could afford at times to sound more conciliatory. But none of the present candidates has his stature," he said.
Nateq-Nouri and Khatami have been vague about their economic platforms, both stressing that development should go with fighting inflation, unemployment and social injustice.

"I think no one among mainstream Iranian politicians questions the need for continued market reforms, but as in any other elections, it is more popular to stress the fight against the reforms' negative consequences," the analyst said.
Many Iranians felt the main difference between the two men was on social issues such as Islamic rules of dress and daily life and cultural matters such as press freedom, analysts said.
Khatami was expected to get support from many women, youths and intellectuals -- who fear a harder social climate under conservatives -- because of his more liberal stands, they said.

Campaigning officially starts only after approved candidates are announced. Unofficial campaigning has been marred by an incident in which hardliners disrupted a speech by Khatami, newspapers said. But the election has so far not been nearly as acrimonious as parliamentary polls last year.
